section_1.title: The Goal: Teaching 'Robo-Chef'
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a neural network through a relatable character. A robot needs to distinguish between a 'Croissant' and a 'Snail'. We start with a high-level overview: data goes in, a guess comes out, and we measure the error.
section_1.example: Visual: Robo-Chef looks at a photo of a snail but shouts 'Delicious Bread!' A 'Disappointment Meter' (Loss Function) hits 90%.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Anatomy of a Neuron
section_2.content: Define 'Weights' and 'Biases' visually. A neuron isn't a complex equation; it's a 'Volume Knob' (Weight) and a 'Sensitivity Switch' (Bias). Signal strength depends on how these knobs are turned.
section_2.example: Animation: Three input wires with knobs labeled 'Swirl Shape', 'Golden Color', and 'Slime Trail'. If the 'Slime' knob is turned up high, the 'Snail' light glows brighter.

section_3.title: The Forward Pass: Making a Guess
section_3.content: Explain the flow of information from left to right. Inputs are multiplied by weights, summed, and passed through an activation function (the 'Threshold Gate').
section_3.example: Visual: Glowing pulses of light travel through layers of knobs. At the final layer, the 'Bread' light flashes weakly while the 'Snail' light stays dark. Result: A wrong prediction.

section_4.title: The Loss Function: Measuring the Gap
section_4.content: Introduce the mathematical concept of 'Error' or 'Loss' as a physical distance. Use a 3D landscape (The Loss Valley) to show that being 'wrong' means being high up on a hill, while being 'right' means being at the bottom of the valley.
section_4.example: Graphic: A ball (Robo-Chef's current state) sitting high on a jagged mountain. The goal is to reach the 'Valley of Correctness' at the bottom.

section_5.title: Intuitive Backpropagation: The Blame Game
section_5.content: This is the core. We work backward from the error. We ask each neuron: 'How much did your knob contribute to this mistake?' This is the visual representation of the Chain Rule.
section_5.example: Animation: The 'Snail' light points a red arrow back at the previous layer's knobs. A knob that was turned too high for 'Slime' gets a 'Turn Me Down!' signal. This is 'Gradient' calculation in action.

section_6.title: Gradient Descent: The Tiny Step
section_6.content: Explain how we use the 'Blame' (Gradients) to actually turn the knobs. Introduce the 'Learning Rate' as the size of the step we take down the mountain.
section_6.example: Visual: A tiny wrench appears and slightly nudges the 'Slime' knob. The ball in the Loss Valley rolls a small step downward. If the step is too big (High Learning Rate), the ball overshoots the valley.

section_7.title: The Iterative Loop: Practice Makes Perfect
section_7.content: Summarize that learning is just repeating the 'Guess -> Blame -> Adjust' cycle thousands of times until the knobs are perfectly tuned.
section_7.example: Time-lapse: Robo-Chef processes 1,000 images of snails and croissants. The knobs spin rapidly, then settle. Finally, a snail is shown, and Robo-Chef confidently says 'Snail!' with 0% Disappointment.

section_6.title: Gradient Descent: The Tiny Step
lecture_lines: We use the calculated blame to adjust the knobs.
A tiny wrench nudges each weight toward the truth.
The "Learning Rate" determines the size of our step.
Too big a step, and we overshoot the valley.
Just right, and we descend safely toward zero error.

Watch as the knobs settle into their perfect positions.
